newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco talks still troubled by liability issue.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco talks still troubled by liability issue.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

Although some state attorneys general have predicted a draft tobacco settlement could be reached in the next few weeks, negotiators are still struggling to find a plan that would protect individuals' rights to sue the industry.
Even as talks are expected to resume this week, some warn the thorny liability issue could cause negotiations to collapse.
"We are at an impasse on the liability issue," said Connecticut Attorney General Richard Blumenthal. "This issue may be well be an insurmountable hurdle to a settlement."

"The industry is beginning to understand we are not willing to tamper with existing basic individual rights and compromise people's right to a day in court," said Blumenthal, who heads a committee considering the civil liability issue. "We're willing to walk away from the table if the industry insists on excessive protection from liability."

A group of attorneys general, plaintiffs lawyers and representatives of the health community began negotiating with the tobacco industry in early April in an effort to resolve mounting litigation against manufacturers in exchange for major health and monetary concessions.

The industry has been sued by 29 attorneys general seeking to recoup Medicaid costs of smokers. Negotiations have been pressured by the fact that Mississippi is scheduled to bring the first of those cases to trial on July 7.

In addition, the industry is facing its first class action trial beginning Monday in Miami. The suit is seeking damages on behalf of about 60,000 flight attendants who allegedly contracted lung diseases and other ailments from secondhand smoke on U.S. passenger jets.

A core group of attorneys general that have sued the industry met with tobacco lawyers in New York last Thursday. They discussed the talks with other attorneys general during a conference call on Friday.
Following the call, Blumenthal told Reuters in a telephone interview he expects meetings with the industry will continue next week.

At issue is whether the parties can agree on a plan that would provide certainty to the industry about the amount of money it would have to pay for smoking related damages, but at the same time protect individuals rights to sue manufacturers.

There have been published reports that the parties have discussed a proposal that would restrict the ability of both current smokers and those with second-hand smoke injuries to sue the industry and that a cap would be placed on possible awards. Reportedly, it would be even tougher for future smokers to win claims.

Although the attorneys general have publicly denied that they have discusssed the monetary part of a settlement, other sources close to the talks have said that the parties have discussed limiting the industry's liability to $4 million annually.
"Conceivably a cap on year-to-year total payments could be considered but not a cap on any individual's recovery," Blumenthal said.
Many attorneys general have said they would be reluctant to approve and might not agree at all to any settlement proposal that would limit individuals' rights to sue the industry.

In addition, some have said they also want provisions that would ensure the tobacco industry is punished and they would not approve a settlement fund that cigarette manufactuers could comfortably pay.
"If it's relatively painless for them and they can move almost effortlessly from this chapter of their history to the next chapter, that would trouble me," said Iowa Attorney General Tom Miller.
"It has to have some punishment aspect to it. It can't be an effortless free ride," he said.
Blumenthal said there would be a strong punitive element in any accord.

"We haven't talked about amounts of money yet, but I feel confident that whatever amount of money is the result of the settlement, if there is one, it will be felt deeply and lastingly by the industry," he said.
